title: Why do tree-based models still outperform deep learning on typical tabular data?

method: Benchmark of tree ensembles vs deep nets on 45 datasets; analysis of inductive biases (irregular functions, uninformative features, rotation invariance)
key_insight: Trees excel because they fit irregular axis-aligned functions and are not rotation-invariant; the band here is two oblique lines through the origin in (guests, aloo_count) space, which axis-aligned splits can only staircase within the observed range.
experiment_inspired: Plot decision regions of a GBM fit on raw (guests, aloo_count) over a grid extended to the test maximum of guests, overlaying the true r=1 and r=2 lines to show where the staircase breaks.

title: Extrapolation is tough for trees!

key_insight: Beyond the training range a tree returns its edge leaf forever, which is exactly why raw-count trees misclassify the ~36% of test weddings whose guests exceed the train maximum.
experiment_inspired: Count test rows outside the train range of guests and of aloo_count; compare raw-feature GBM predictions with ratio-rule predictions on those rows (disagreement rate as an extrapolation-error proxy).

key_insight: linear_tree=True lets raw-count boosting extrapolate linearly, but a band in aloo_count/guests is not linear in raw counts, and monotone constraints cannot encode a non-monotone band, so these are diagnostics rather than a substitute for the ratio feature.
experiment_inspired: Compare LightGBM on raw counts vs linear_tree=True on raw counts vs LightGBM on the ratio, scored on a guests-based extrapolation split.
notes: URL verified via WebSearch and WebFetch (linear_tree and monotone_constraints text checked, incl. that monotone constraints do not apply to the leaf linear models).

experiment_inspired: Create d = max(1 - r, 0, r - 2); fit XGBoost with monotone_constraints=-1 on d and compare CV and extrapolation-split accuracy with the hard rule.

experiment_inspired: Fit a flexible raw-feature model with and without density-ratio weights (from an adversarial train-vs-test classifier) and check whether weighting closes the gap to the ratio rule on an extrapolation split.
